newsitem.title: UK: Antimony firm, cobalt nervy in minor metals.
newsitem.headline: Antimony firm, cobalt nervy in minor metals.

text.p: Antimony prices continued to push higher in the minor industrial metals market, as nearby tightness continued to grip the market, traders said.

Elsewhere, there was uncertainty in cobalt over African metal supplies and the outcome of the DLA tender. Chrome prices were slightly lower, but generally conditions were still "gearing up" after the Easter holiday, they said.
"It has been ticking over, certainly, but there has not been that much real trade to speak off from where I'm sitting," one said.
In antimony, the market gained ground after a meeting of Chinese smelters and miners decided to limit production to boost the market.
Traders said the Chinese were also withdrawing from the market in some cases, which in tandem with tight nearby availability was squeezing prompt prices.
"The Chinese are cranking the market - they are holding back at the moment," one trader said.
Others reported good consumer business in Europe and the U.S.
"There is upward pressure coming from China, and it is dragging consumers into the market," another trader said.
In the short-term, the next move depends on consumer activity, and if there is sustained end-user offtake prices could push above $2,500 and head higher yet - perhaps the $3,000/tonne level.
In cobalt, prices were holding steady with traders hearing that Zaire's Gecamines had formally withdrawn from selling.
The other African producer Zambia was also said to be shying away from the spot market, although this could be construed as a measure to boost prices further, they said.

In the U.S., meanwhile, the Court of Federal Claims is due to hear a request Thursday afternoon for a temporary restraining order on the DLA's proposed sale of one million lbs of high grade cobalt by sealed bid.

Last Friday, the DLA postponed the opening of bids for the sale until April 7 after a request for a temporary restraining order to stop the sale filed by Minor Metals Inc, also known as Metal Resources Group Ltd.
Some traders here were unhappy over the continued delay in the stockpile offerings and moves to have negotiated bids.
"This is getting to be a farce - they should insist on fixed bids," one European trader said.

Chrome prices were a shade softer, as the tightness in the market eased slightly. Russian material has started to come through after a barren first quarter, while there is also more Chinese chrome available.
"It is still tight, but there a just a few more units coming through now," one trader said.
In other metals, germanium was losing ground, with the market pressured by offerings of stockpile material.
